Cobble

KOB-uhl -- from Middle English, likely related to cob ('a rounded lump'); origin uncertain. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To cobble to put something together roughly or hastily, often from whatever materials are available.

When the projector failed five minutes before the assembly, the AV club had to cobble together a backup using three laptops and a bedsheet screen.

Worked Example

With the venue's sound system dead an hour before the show, the stagehands cobbled together a working PA system from two guitar amps and a karaoke machine.

The replacement PA system wasn't carefully engineered -- it was quickly thrown together from whatever equipment was on hand, which is exactly what it means to cobble something together.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

improvise: to create or assemble something on the spot, without preparation

patch: to put together in a makeshift or temporary way

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

engineer: to design and build something carefully and precisely

craft: to make something skillfully and with care

Where it sits · how much you build from scratch — patch → cobble → improvise

patch vs. cobble: They patched together a plan for dinner using whatever was left in the fridge.

improvise vs. cobble: Improvise goes further than cobble: to cobble a plan together is to build roughly from scraps you already have, while improvising means inventing an entire segment from nothing, on the spot.

Build the Word

The pieces

Put it together

Put it together: Cobble's exact origin is a bit of a mystery -- it likely comes from cob, an old word for a rounded lump, though how that turned into 'assemble roughly' isn't entirely clear. A cobbled-together plan is knocked into shape from whatever lumps of material happen to be lying around.

Use the root in a new word: cobblestone

Use the root in a new word: cobblestone: A cobblestone street is paved with rounded stones -- cobbles -- that share this same uncertain root.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Cobble almost always appears in the phrase cobble together, and it usually implies a rushed, improvised solution rather than a carefully planned one -- often said with a hint of admiration for pulling something off under pressure.
